title: A Tiny Robot That Swims With Living Muscles
summary:
Most swimming robots carry a motor. A new robot from MIT moves through the water in a different way: it is powered by a thin layer of living muscle cells.

The tiny robot has a soft gel body about the size of a stick of gum, with two fins coated in muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. The cells were genetically changed so they squeeze, or contract, whenever light shines on them.

By aiming light at one fin or the other, the researchers can make the fins flap and push the robot forward. Shining light more or less often, and choosing which fin gets it, lets the team steer the robot and control its speed.

In experiments, the robot swam and turned through an underwater maze. At its fastest, it covered about four times its own body length in one minute. That is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, but about the pace of a cow shark cruising through the ocean.

'It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air,' said study author Ritu Raman, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. 'The robot's quite strong, given its size.'

The study, published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials, is the first demonstration of a very thin robot that can travel from place to place using living muscle tissue. Machines that mix living tissue with human-made materials are called biohybrid robots.

Raman says thin designs could be cheaper to build and move more efficiently than bulky biohybrid robots made from millions of cells. One day, robots powered by living muscle might do delicate jobs in places too fragile for ordinary machines, because living tissue is soft, responds to its surroundings, and can heal itself.
why_it_matters: Mixing living tissue with machines could create softer robots that move efficiently and work safely in fragile places that ordinary machines might damage.
